capabilities: audio/ui ships the behaviour of a DAW editor with no styles: Sequencer and PianoRoll handle painting, dragging, resizing, selection and keyboard control, and expose state as data-* attributes and CSS variables. Playheads follow a live source written straight to the DOM, so a 16th-note clock never re-renders React.

name: Snd
capabilities: Snd (Dentsu) pairs each UI event — tap, select, toggle on/off, swipe, notification, caution, celebration — with a sound composed for it, in three kits by different sound designers (sine, piano, industrial). One call per interaction, e.g. snd.playToggleOn(); switching kits changes the whole texture. Sounds: free-use terms at snd.dev, © their designers.

name: SVGuitar
capabilities: SVGuitar draws fully configurable chord diagrams (fingers, barres, positions, tunings, colors) as SVG, and one setting, style: 'handdrawn', swaps its renderer for roughjs wobbly ink with hatched finger dots and an embedded Patrick Hand font. Every element carries class names like .string-3 or .finger-string-2, so you can style and animate a chart string by string with CSS.

name: Fretboard.js
capabilities: Fretboard.js renders a guitar neck as plain SVG with d3-selection and knows the theory: renderScale() returns every position tagged with note, interval, degree and whether it sits in a CAGED or three-notes-per-string box, so styling by interval is one style() call per degree. Dots carry those tags as CSS classes too, and fretboard.on() maps pointer coordinates back to string and fret.

name: VexFlow
capabilities: VexFlow lays out real engraved notation: grand staves, braces, key signatures, auto-stemmed beams, dots, and accidentals computed against the key, all drawn with the bundled SMuFL Bravura font. Here every key you press is quantized and engraved live, with bar lines appearing as measures fill; when idle it plays Petzold's Minuet in G and Ode to Joy.

name: alphaTab
capabilities: alphaTab engraves standard notation and tablature from Guitar Pro files or its alphaTex text format, then plays them through a SoundFont synth in a web worker with the cursor and note highlights locked to playback. Here a hand-written alphaTex arrangement of the anonymous 'Romanza' is restyled for dark mode through alphaTab's rendering resources, with track switching, speed, metronome and count-in. Audio uses the bundled SONiVOX soundfont (Apache-2.0); nothing loads from a CDN.

name: @web-kits/audio
capabilities: Clicks, ticks, pops and whooshes are described as plain JSON-like objects (source, envelope, filter, layers) and synthesized live with Web Audio, so a whole sound kit weighs a few hundred bytes. Here every control has its own micro-sound; tweak pitch, decay and sweep to hear the edit and watch the definition and its offline-rendered waveform update.

name: Orca
capabilities: Hundred Rabbits' Orca is a programming language drawn on a monospaced grid: clocks, euclid gates and random operators bang their neighbours, and a ':' cell fires a MIDI note. This runs the unmodified web client with a Web MIDI shim feeding a small WebAudio synth, so the patch's drums, bass, lead and E-operator 'comets' play in the browser.

name: Patchcab
capabilities: Each module is a Svelte faceplate wrapping Tone.js nodes, and a patch is just 'output jack -> input jack', so a whole rack serialises to plain JSON. Cables are drawn as sagging catenary SVG curves you can grab and re-plug while the audio graph rewires live.

name: The Endless Acid Banger
capabilities: An art project by David Whiting (Vitling), CC BY 4.0: two TB-303-style voices and a 909 kit in plain TypeScript + WebAudio, with an autopilot that rewrites patterns, mutes drums and wanders the knobs while you watch the notes. Here vendored with a synthesized drum kit instead of samples and a restyled, phone-friendly layout.

name: Viktor NV-1
capabilities: Viktor NV-1 is a complete subtractive synth in plain Web Audio: three oscillators, mixer, ladder-style filter with its own envelope, LFO, delay and convolution reverb, driven by MIDI bytes. Its engine ships separately on npm, so you can put your own front panel on it. Here, brushed metal, wood cheeks and knob sprites from the original MIT repo drive the real engine, and all 64 factory patches are included.

name: Glicol
capabilities: Glicol patches are terse chains like `seq 60 _ 60 >> bd 0.2`, with `~ref` chains modulating any parameter, all run by a GC-free Rust engine inside an AudioWorklet. The engine parses and swaps graphs live: a typo reports line and column and the old graph keeps playing. Every sound here comes from synth nodes, with no samples.

name: ZzFXM
capabilities: A whole song is one nested array of ZzFX instrument numbers, note patterns and a sequence, and zzfxM() renders it to raw sample buffers in a few hundred milliseconds. The two original songs here are under 5 KB of JSON each and expand to about 5 MB of PCM, which is why js13k games use it. The demo renders each channel in a worker so every voice gets its own scope, meter and mute.

name: abcjs
capabilities: abcjs parses ABC, the plain-text folk-music notation, and engraves it as real SVG sheet music: clefs, beams, voltas, chord symbols, auto line-wrapping. It also flattens the tune into timed note events, so a cursor can bounce across the score while each note maps back to the exact characters in your source.

name: Pitchy
capabilities: Pitchy runs the McLeod Pitch Method (FFT autocorrelation + normalized square difference) on a plain Float32Array and returns [pitch, clarity] — no AudioWorklet or framework required. Here it reads a synthesized, vibrato-laden sung phrase every frame to drive a cents arc meter with a hero note readout, a strobe band, a scrolling pitch trail and live stats (findPitch time, rms error vs the synth's true pitch); tap 'use mic' to tune your own voice.

name: webaudio-pianoroll
capabilities: <webaudio-pianoroll> gives you a complete note editor (draw, drag, resize, area-select, loop markers, playhead) as a single tag, with every colour exposed as an attribute and playback scheduled against any AudioContext clock. Here colnote is fed a per-row gradient so bass, chords and lead get their own bevelled lane colours, and a tiny hand-written WebAudio synth plays the callbacks.

name: Chrome Music Lab
capabilities: Mark Lundin's Sound Waves experiment, running from its original Tone.js + WebGL bundle: a floor of air particles bunches into glowing compressions as you play the piano, tinted with Chrome Music Lab's colour for each note, and the lens follows a single particle to draw its sine trace. The bundle is untouched; the wrapper restyles its shaders and keyboard at runtime.

name: Pink Trombone
capabilities: A physical model of the throat, mouth and nose: a 44-segment waveguide driven by an LF glottal pulse, so moving the tongue or closing the lips changes the sound. This package strips Thapen's UI and exposes normalized vowel, constriction, pitch and nasality controls, and lets you run several voices at once. The demo redraws his pink tract from the library's live diameters. It babbles words on its own until you take over, and choir mode stacks three trombones.

name: ElevenLabs UI
capabilities: The Orb is a WebGL shader sphere whose polar ovals and noisy rings react to separate input and output volumes, so listening, thinking and talking each move differently. Here a synthesized formant 'voice' drives it alongside the registry's BarVisualizer and ShimmeringText. You install it by copying source into your project with the shadcn CLI.

Matrix is an SVG dot-matrix display with glowing LEDs. It ships with ready-made frame sets (digits, loader, pulse, wave, snake) and a vu() spectrum mode. This demo builds it into a phosphor display device: an AnalyserNode on a synthesized chiptune loop drives the VU, the registry's Waveform draws a level strip, and you can switch the clock and animation presets.

name: chiptune3
capabilities: Plays real tracker modules through libopenmpt (wasm) running in an AudioWorklet and exposes the parsed pattern data, order list and sample names. Here it drives a scrolling 4-channel pattern view and stereo scope, and decodeAll() pre-renders a whole-song waveform before any user gesture. Both songs are original modules generated in code for this demo (CC0).

name: ZzFX
capabilities: Every sound effect is one short array of numbers. Unchanged values are left out, so a whole coin pickup is 43 bytes of code, a favourite in js13k games. Sixteen pads show their real waveforms built by ZZFX.buildSamples; edit any of the 21 parameters to redraw it and update the copyable zzfx(...[...]) string.

name: Chromatone
capabilities: Chromatone gives each of the 12 pitch classes a fixed hue, so chords become color sets. pitchColor/noteColor color single notes, and chromaColorMix blends a whole chord into one color. Here the wheel, polygon, center disc, background and piano all take their colors from those calls.

name: Sandspiel
capabilities: Max Bittker's Rust cellular automaton runs 19 elements that react with each other: lava cools to stone, plants climb wood, cloners copy whatever touches them. A sand.glsl shader gives each cell its soft pastel colour and noise. A GPU fluid sim underneath carries fire's updraft and lets you blow wind across the canvas. This demo runs the real crate compiled to wasm with upstream's own shaders.
installs: git clone https://github.com/MaxBittker/sandspiel && cd sandspiel/crate && cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release && wasm-bindgen --target web --out-dir pkg target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/sandtable.wasm

name: binjgb
capabilities: binjgb is Ben Smith's cycle-accurate Game Boy emulator: an 88 KB wasm file with a plain C API for frames, audio, save states and a delta-compressed rewind buffer. Here it runs in a CSS-drawn DMG. A bot plays by reading the game's RAM, and when it dies it rewinds the tape and tries again. Game: Tobu Tobu Girl by Tangram Games (code MIT, assets CC BY 4.0).

name: JSNES
capabilities: JSNES gives you a frame buffer and audio samples per frame, and you decide how to draw them. Here each frame is uploaded to a WebGL shader that adds tube curvature, scanlines, an aperture grille, bloom and channel-change static inside a wood-grain TV. Three public-domain or permissively licensed homebrew carts: Lawn Mower and Lan Master by Shiru, RHDE by Damian Yerrick.

name: Decker
capabilities: Decker rebuilds the HyperCard idea for the web: stacks of cards with buttons, fields and canvases, dithered 1-bit paint tools, sound, and the small Lil scripting language. Web-Decker is one self-contained HTML file per deck, so it embeds anywhere with no server and keeps working offline. This demo runs the real upstream build on six of John Earnest's example decks.
installs: git clone https://github.com/JohnEarnest/Decker && cd Decker && make web-decker

name: Octo
capabilities: Octo is John Earnest's toolchain for the 1977 CHIP-8 virtual machine and its XO-CHIP extension (4 colours, 128x64, sampled audio), and it is what the annual Octojam game jam is built on. Its emulator core is two plain scripts you can drive yourself. This cabinet runs 23 CC0 Octojam games from the chip8Archive with each cart's original palette and quirks, Octo's six palette presets, attract mode and a touch hex keypad.

name: Phaser 4
capabilities: Phaser 4 rebuilds the renderer around filters: any camera or game object gets internal/external filter lists (Glow, Blur, Barrel, Pixelate, Vignette, ColorMatrix, Bokeh, Displacement...) plus composite Actions like AddEffectBloom. This attract-mode brick-breaker stacks bloom, vignette and a barrel pulse on the camera, glows the bricks, ball and paddle, and fires pixelate and hue-sweep bursts on combos and wave clears. Textures are drawn procedurally, and the chips toggle each filter live.

name: Excalibur
capabilities: Excalibur's pixelArt mode keeps sprites crisp while they move at sub-pixel positions and the camera eases, so you don't have to snap to integer coordinates. Its PostProcessor API takes your own GLSL fragment shader and runs it over the finished frame. Here that shader adds a curved tube, scanlines, chromatic aberration and a vignette to an endless attract-mode run. The scene also uses arcade physics, one-way platforms, ParallaxComponent layers, sprite-sheet animations and particle bursts. All art is generated at runtime.

name: SpessaSynth
capabilities: A full General MIDI engine (SF2/SF3/DLS, reverb, chorus, 16+ channels) that runs off the main thread, plus a core that can author SoundFonts and MIDI files in the browser. Here the 214 KB SoundFont and all three songs are generated in JS with its own BasicSoundBank and MIDIBuilder APIs; the meters read the synth's 16 per-channel outputs.

name: WASM-4
capabilities: WASM-4 runs games from any language that compiles to WebAssembly under hard limits: a 160×160 screen, a 4-colour palette, 64 KB of memory and four sound channels, all driven through memory-mapped registers and a 2-bit framebuffer. This original 15.5 KB Rust cart runs in the stock web runtime. It cross-fades its own PALETTE registers between eight palettes, and the page reads them back to tint itself.

name: TIC-80
capabilities: TIC-80 is a tiny virtual console with fixed limits: 240×136 pixels, a 16-colour palette, 4 sound channels, and code, sprites, map and sound packed into a single .tic cartridge. This demo is an original Lua cart running in the official WebAssembly player. The sky and ground gradients come from swapping palette entries on every scanline in BDR(), so the screen shows more than 16 colours at once.
installs: download the HTML player from https://github.com/nesbox/TIC-80/releases (tic80-v1.3-players.tar.gz → lua/tic80.js + tic80lua.wasm)

name: Pyxel
capabilities: Pyxel deliberately limits you to a 16-colour palette, 4 sound channels and 256x256 sprite banks, then gives you a tiny Python API (blt, dither, rotate/scale blits, sounds[].set note strings). This original side-scroller is plain Python running in CPython-on-wasm (Pyodide) with Pyxel's Rust core compiled to wasm32, all self-hosted.

name: Uxn5
capabilities: Uxn is a 32-opcode stack machine and Varvara is the tiny computer built around it: a 4-colour palette that each ROM sets, 2-bit sprites on two layers, and devices for the screen, mouse and controller. Uxn5 runs those ROMs in the browser and fits in a few kB of plain script plus a wasm core. This demo boots an original Uxntal toy, 100r's Catclock and the card game Donsol, all built with the official drifloon assembler.

name: v86
capabilities: v86 emulates a whole PC (CPU, VGA, floppy controller, PIT, keyboard) and JIT-compiles guest x86 code to WebAssembly, so real BIOSes and operating systems boot in a tab. Here SeaBIOS boots nanochess's 512-byte bootOS from a floppy image assembled in JS at runtime. An autopilot reads the emulated VGA text buffer to play Bricks, then the demo moves on to a raycaster, bootBASIC and a pi calculator.

name: PuzzleScript
capabilities: PuzzleScript games are plain text: 5x5 pixel sprites, sfxr sound seeds, collision layers and pattern-rewrite rules like [ > Player | Crate ] -> [ > Player | > Crate ]. This original 4-level game runs on the unmodified engine; the source sits beside it and each rule line lights up as the engine applies it.
installs: git clone https://github.com/increpare/PuzzleScript (or File > Export standalone HTML on puzzlescript.net)

name: LittleJS
capabilities: LittleJS draws batched WebGL sprites, runs a ParticleEmitter system, plays ZzFX sound and adds a Shadertoy-style post-process pass, and the whole engine is small enough for a game jam. Here every hit sets off additive particle bursts and camera shake, and the bloom, chromatic split and scanlines come from the engine's own post-process effect functions. Nothing in the demo is loaded from an image file.
